# Dhanañjāni Sutta (MN 97 (PTS MN ii 184))

**ID:** MN 97 (PTS MN ii 184)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Dhanañjāni Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Dhanañjāni
**PTS:** MN ii 184
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhanañjāni Sutta* (MN 97) records a renowned discourse given by the Venerable Sāriputta concerning ethics, lay obligations, and deathbed guidance [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Gaffney 2003]. While dwelling in the Southern Hills, Sāriputta learns from a visiting monk that the brahmin Dhānañjāni has taken up a corrupt livelihood as a tax collector, exploiting both king and subjects [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Langer 2007]. Sāriputta confronts him, explaining that multifarious householder obligations—such as providing for family, dependents, and social duties—cannot excuse unethical conduct or protect one from the kammic consequences of unwholesome deeds [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Sayers 2008]. Later, when Dhānañjāni falls terminally ill, Sāriputta visits his deathbed and guides him to cultivate the four *brahmavihāra*s (sublime attitudes), enabling his rebirth in the Brahma world [Tan 2002; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Aronson 1980]. Following Dhānañjāni's death, the Buddha mildly rebukes Sāriputta for having departed "while there was still more to be done" (*sati uttarakaraṇīye*), as Dhānañjāni had the capacity for higher supramundane attainment rather than rebirth in an inferior Brahma world [Tan 2002; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Aronson 1980].

The text's established parallel is preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 27), where comparative studies highlight several narrative and doctrinal divergences, such as variations in sickness similes and the depiction of ritual duties and blessings [Anālayo 2016; Radich 2007]. DharmaNexus aligns MN 97 with this *Madhyama-āgama* version, as well as with the Tibetan *Karmaśataka* (D340) and Sanskrit passages in the *Carmavastu* and *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse, particularly in deathbed and pastoral formulas shared with the *Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta* (MN 143), the *Channovāda Sutta* (MN 144), and the *Sotāpatti Saṁyutta* (SN 55) [DharmaNexus].
